clinicalPearls: A net-like, reticular violaceous mottling of the skin caused by altered flow within the dermal vascular network.
The physiological form (cutis marmorata) produces complete, symmetrical rings that reverse with warming and is common and benign in infants and young women.
Livedo racemosa, by contrast, shows broken, irregular, asymmetrical rings that persist on warming and signals an underlying vasculopathy.
Livedo racemosa is an important cutaneous marker of Sneddon syndrome (with cerebrovascular events) and of antiphospholipid syndrome.
Secondary causes include vasculitis such as polyarteritis nodosa, cholesterol embolisation, calciphylaxis, hyperviscosity, cryoglobulinaemia and certain drugs.
Reversibility with warming and the regularity of the pattern help separate the benign from the pathological forms.
When biopsy is needed it should be deep and taken from the pale centre of the network rather than the blue rim, where the culprit vessel is more likely to be sampled.
reference.pathophysiology: The reticular pattern reflects the cone-shaped territories supplied by ascending dermal arterioles: deoxygenated blood pooling in the venous plexus at the periphery of each cone produces the bluish reticulate network. Anything that reduces inflow or increases stasis at the cone periphery accentuates the pattern, including vasospasm, luminal obstruction from thrombosis, emboli or hyperviscosity, and inflammatory vessel-wall disease. In the physiological form the change is purely vasomotor and reverses with warming, whereas in pathological livedo racemosa fixed vascular occlusion or wall damage produces a persistent, irregular pattern.
additionalDifferentials: Livedo racemosa secondary to systemic disease
Reticulate erythema of connective tissue disease
additionalInvestigations: Antiphospholipid antibody testing (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti-beta-2-glycoprotein-I antibodies)
Autoimmune screen including antinuclear antibodies and ANCA
Deep skin biopsy taken from the centre of the pale area
Screening for an embolic source and a thrombophilia workup
Neuroimaging when Sneddon syndrome is suspected
redFlags: Neurological symptoms such as stroke or transient ischaemic attack suggesting Sneddon syndrome
Systemic features of vasculitis or embolic disease
A fixed, irregular racemosa pattern that does not resolve with warming
reference.prognosis: The physiological form is entirely benign, whereas the prognosis of pathological livedo depends on the underlying disorder, with thrombotic risk in antiphospholipid and Sneddon syndromes being of particular concern.
pitfalls: Dismissing pathological livedo racemosa as benign cutis marmorata.
Taking a superficial or peripherally placed biopsy that misses the affected vessel.
Failing to test for antiphospholipid syndrome in a young patient presenting with livedo and stroke.
Attributing drug-induced or embolic livedo to a primary skin disorder.
management: Reassure and advise warmth with avoidance of cold for benign physiological cutis marmorata, which needs no specific treatment
Identify and treat the underlying cause, distinguishing benign livedo reticularis from pathological livedo racemosa
Give antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy where associated with antiphospholipid syndrome or Sneddon syndrome and thrombotic risk
Treat specific secondary causes, such as immunosuppression for polyarteritis nodosa or management of cholesterol embolisation, calciphylaxis and cryoglobulinaemia
Address modifiable vascular risk factors and withdraw any causative drugs
Investigate and monitor for cerebrovascular events when Sneddon syndrome is suspected
Refer to dermatology, rheumatology or neurology according to the underlying disorder
